title: Inside police plans to share intelligence and crime data across the UK
raw_text:
UK police are developing a national service for sharing local intelligence and police force data across the law enforcement and justice estate.

Announced by the National Police Chiefs’ Council (NPCC) earlier this year, the National Data Integration and Exploitation Service (NDIES) will allow local police forces to access and share data, including local force intelligence and digital forensics, from across the country.

Privacy campaigners have raised concerns that the project could facilitate artificial intelligence (AI)-powered analysis of bulk datasets of personal information which, when considered alongside facial recognition and other forms of real-time tracking, shows how “powerful” state surveillance apparatus is.

A “police data factory” within NDIES will incorporate data from over 50 law enforcement agencies, the Home Office, the Ministry of Justice, and “other” partners to provide them with access to a vast network of data for “analytical and reporting purposes”. These government departments will not be able to see operational data or intelligence itself, according to the NPCC.

Computer Weekly can also reveal exclusive details about key data exploitation systems used by several police forces expected to “plug into” NDIES datasets, including:

  • A planned national roll-out of software that will facilitate deep analysis of forensically extracted mobile phone data.
  • Internal Bedfordshire Police memos that admit there is a “medium risk” that a system provided by the US-based data analytics firm Palantir will potentially process personal data for purposes that are neither proportionate nor necessary.
  • Datasets feeding Bedfordshire Police’s Palantir system contain more than 1,000 records on people who haven’t been charged with crimes.

The National Data Integration and Exploitation Service

The National Data and Analytics Office (NDAO) within the NPCC is delivering the NDIES in collaboration with the Home Office. Kate Fisher-Stevens, director of the NDAO, has said the aim is “not to create a single national platform, collect more data or share it unnecessarily” but to “ensure data can be collated when necessary”.

“The creation of a centralised data infrastructure that supports cross-force, cross-system data sharing will be pivotal to that aim – creating a single version of the truth, with time, resource and subsequent cost significantly reduced,” she said.

In a pre-market engagement tender published last year, the capabilities for the NDIES were expected to cost between £75m and £250m over five years. Although no suppliers have been announced yet, documents obtained by Computer Weekly indicate that Palantir’s Foundry product is one of the preferred choices to meet these needs due to government and policing “interest”.

Design proposals for the delivery of police data integration and exploitation systems have also included plans to integrate criminal justice data with the Single Unique Identifiers being piloted by the Department for Education for child safeguarding.

Campaign groups have previously raised concerns with the Single Unique Identifiers as a child protection and crime reduction safeguarding initiative. The Traveller Movement, which advocates for Romany, Roma and Irish travellers, provided written evidence to Parliament warning that tracking children through these identifiers “could be perceived as an infringement on the privacy and autonomy of families who have historically faced marginalisation and excessive surveillance by public authorities”.

When asked if this has the potential to bring data on all school children into the hands of the police, the NPCC deferred the question to the Home Office, which in turn did not provide any answers.

The NDIES framework has been designed so that analytical tools can “plug into” national policing datasets to exploit the data. According to documents obtained by Computer Weekly under Freedom of Information laws, these tools appear to include an in-house system known as Prometheus and systems designed by Palantir and BAE Systems.

Exploitation of local policing intelligence and digital forensics, such as data extracted from mobile phones, will be central to the police’s plans, according to specifications seen by Computer Weekly.

A spokesperson and legal researcher from digital rights campaign group Privacy International said: “This is a step up in terms of how much data is being shared, and what forces across the board will be able to do with the data. It also opens up the possibility for using the data for predictive analytics.

“The amount of information that they can now collect and process, as they’re no longer having to dedicate human resources to this type of investigatory work, is alarming.”

Prometheus and Palantir Nectar: Data exploitation tools

Two key tools under development by the police are expected to play a key role in generating data and intelligence shared under the NDIES.

Computer Weekly has exclusive details about Prometheus, an “intelligence-only” system developed to aid analysis of digital devices seized from suspects.

Unlike tools such as Cellebrite, which decrypt and extract data from seized devices, Prometheus allows investigators to derive insights from the extracted data by cross-referencing it with other police systems. Personal data that police extract from mobile devices includes photos, text conversations and internet logs.

This allows investigators to build a picture of a case by identifying links and patterns between the data and existing police intelligence records. The outputs of intelligence-only systems are generally not admissible as evidence in court, however.

It is used primarily in child sexual abuse investigations so far, although there are plans to deploy it across a “far wider range” of offences.

Details of the system are considered so sensitive that the NPCC has not disclosed which five police forces are currently using it.

The NDAO’s Fisher-Stevens told Computer Weekly that a “number of forces have been involved in the development of Prometheus”, but she wouldn’t specify which, as this would “influence criminal tactics and significantly impact the interception of child sexual abuse”.

The NPCC refused to release details of the project’s collaborators, citing Freedom of Information Act (FOIA) exemptions that prevent the disclosure of information provided by or relating to the security bodies – for example, the National Crime Agency (NCA) or GCHQ.

The ultimate aim with Prometheus is national roll-out and availability to all police forces. It is currently live on the National Police Capability Environment, a web-based Microsoft Azure cloud platform.

Another tool currently being piloted by British police forces is Palantir Nectar. Bedfordshire Police contracted the US-based analytics firm Palantir Technologies to provide this service. It connects existing police data sources under a unified view, with underlying applications allowing investigators to exploit mobile phone data, profile individuals and process sensitive personal data with artificial intelligence.

It is built on the Palantir Foundry framework, the same system used in the NHS Federated Data Platform, which is an operating system that organises data and integrates it into specific analytics applications.

One application within Nectar called “Project Retrace” allows the police to map out locations an individual has visited based on troves of forensically extracted phone data, according to FOIA disclosures to Computer Weekly.

A Bedfordshire Police spokesperson refused to explain how this works. It’s unclear if the geolocation is based on cached data from apps that record your on-device location, by examining IP addresses that your phone has connected to, or through phone mast triangulation.

A spokesperson from digital rights group Privacy International said the police collect this data “through mobile phone extraction, cloud extraction, requesting information from mobile networks, and by purchasing data from data brokers”.

They added: “Many police forces hold this data not only from suspects, but from potential victims and witnesses of crimes.”

Several other applications within Palantir Nectar make use of forensically analysed device data. One has been specifically designed to support a national policing operation targeting Western Balkan organised crime and immigration offences. It appears that the AI has been trained to “recognise images of cocaine and cannabis” found in extracted devices, according to previous reports.

Another application within Nectar provides “AI-supported mobile phone analysis and translation” of extracted device data.

The system also analyses sensitive personal data, including people’s political opinions, religious beliefs and sexual orientations, according to previous reports.

Computer Weekly has obtained an equality impact assessment for Nectar, created before any contracts had been signed with Palantir. It does not mention people whose data could be trawled, only impacts on the workforce using the tool.

Concerns have been raised that “like any AI system, the outputs depend on the data fed into it” that “reflect historic and existing biases within these institutions and across wider society”, according to Alamara Khwaja Bettum, executive director of civil liberties charity Statewatch.

This will likely “lead to over-policing and criminalisation of marginalised communities, particularly racialised groups, migrants and people from low-income neighbourhoods”.

According to internal police documents obtained by Computer Weekly, the force has also not fully mitigated the risks of personal data being processed where the purposes are neither proportionate nor necessary. The volume of personal data processed may also be “excessive”.

One of the data sources for Palantir Nectar – a system called Athena – contained more than 1,000 records for individuals in 2025 who had not been charged with any crimes, according to freedom of information disclosures to Computer Weekly. Any of this sensitive personal data could be analysed by Nectar’s AI processing if investigators were to choose to do so.

Privacy International said that this risks “disproportionate and unnecessary use of personal data, inaccuracy, data security, and the rights of freedoms of individuals”, which Bedfordshire Police has itself acknowledged in internal documents.

The campaign group continued that the police force’s decision to use Nectar to “expand its surveillance capabilities by exploiting deeply intrusive data about individuals, without concern for [Palantir’s] human rights record, and without fully explaining how the data will be used or how many people this project will affect, raises serious legal and ethical concerns”.

Bedfordshire Police is leading the Palantir Nectar pilot within the Eastern Regional Special Operations Unit (ERSOU), a joint policing unit tackling serious organised crime and terrorism. Cambridgeshire and Hertfordshire constabularies have access to the platform through Bedfordshire Police. These forces, alongside Essex, Kent, Norfolk and Suffolk constabularies, make up the rest of the ERSOU. The pilot is in preparation for a national roll-out of the software.

The pilot is being partially audited by Accenture. This same consultancy firm has recently announced a “global strategic partnership” with Palantir, acquired a company that helps organisations implement Palantir’s software, and is part of the same consortium earning from the multimillion-pound NHS contract.

Representatives for Accenture acknowledged Computer Weekly’s queries but failed to respond.

Bedfordshire Police did not answer questions about whether it considered a conflict of interest in having Accenture audit its pilot, given that the firm could stand to gain from Palantir obtaining further government contracts, but a spokesperson said the force is also evaluating the project internally.

Bedfordshire Police said it is “imperative” that police systems evolve to “provide a service the public expects” given the changing policing landscape. The number of domestic violence disclosures has also trebled as a result of the Palantir Nectar pilot, according to the force. An ethics panel composed of police officials and academics is providing “independent scrutiny” of AI use, while the police and crime commissioner is also establishing an Artificial Intelligence Advisory Ethics Panel.

A Palantir spokesperson said the firm is “proud” the software is fighting crime. “But that is what it is – software. How that software is used to process data is entirely under the control of the customer. Critically, use of the software does not involve acquiring any data that the customer in question doesn’t already have access to – it simply organises that data in a way that enables faster, better decision-making.”

Palantir also confirmed to Computer Weekly that its software has been used by the US military for airstrike targeting in Iran.

“Palantir has developed its technologies by testing them in war-torn countries and using them in the genocide in Palestine,” according to Romain Lanneau, a legal consultant at Statewatch. “Based on that alone, the UK should consider any collaboration with Palantir highly unethical.”

Leicestershire Police is also leading a Palantir Nectar trial within the East Midlands Special Operations Unit (EMSOU), which includes Derbyshire, Lincolnshire, Northamptonshire and Nottinghamshire Police.

London mayor Sadiq Khan recently blocked the Metropolitan Police’s £50m deal with Palantir as the proposal had not “ensured or demonstrated value for money”, although the force has been able to continue using it for the next year.

Police plans to integrate IT systems

Police chiefs had previously expressed concerns about reliance on the multiplicity of commercial and in-house platforms such as Palantir Nectar, Prometheus and BAE Systems’ Intelligence Lead Assessment Service, and existing systems such as the Police National Database, which risk “excessive costs” and “architectural incoherence” given that they would all be using the same data, according to documents obtained by Computer Weekly.

The solution, therefore, was to bring all of the police’s data exploitation and collation tools under one roof.

“The National Data and Analytics Office is working to centralise the way in which forces utilise data and procure data exploitation technology – to reduce duplicated investment and again, protect forces against the risks [mentioned],” the NDAO’s Fisher-Stevens told Computer Weekly.

Following on from London City Hall blocking the Met’s £50m contract with Palantir, commissioner Mark Rowley warned against the constraints of public procurement policy on the police’s ability to deploy emerging technology effectively. Rowley said the force stands to gain from being able to “connect” and “spot patterns at the touch of a button” across the force’s 2,200 datasets held in over 600 systems.

The NDIES appears to answer this concern, giving the police access to a wide range of national intelligence in an organised way. Yet the underlying risks raised by campaign groups on biases within the data and the invasive nature of collection remain. “The question is whether it can possibly be necessary and proportionate,” according to Privacy International.

title: Technology teams to be hit by Visa’s 7% jobs cull
raw_text:
Visa will cut 7% of its workforce and increase the use of artificial intelligence (AI) to “evolve” how it works, according to an internal memo to staff.

In his message to over 34,000 employees, reported by Bloomberg, Visa CEO Ryan McInerney said its technology and product teams will primarily be affected by the 2,600 job cuts.

The CEO wrote: “I have deep conviction that we are doing what is right for Visa, our clients and our partners as we continue to focus on driving efficiency across the company in order to reinvest in our highest potential opportunities.”

He told staff that AI is being used to change how employees work. “To capture the opportunities ahead and best position Visa to lead this transformation, we must continue evolving how we work,” wrote McInerney. “AI is also helping to accelerate this evolution and shape the way work gets done at Visa.”

Quoting a person with knowledge of the company’s decision, Bloomberg reported that AI is not the only driver of the job cuts, with Visa keen to reinvest in “consumer payments, commercial and money-movement solutions and value-added services, which include stablecoin, cross-border and business-to-business offerings”.

According to an independent benchmarking report in February, AI has already become institutionalised at Visa, and the firm is leading the way in the technology’s application in the payments sector.

The report from benchmarking company Evident ranked Visa number one in its AI index for payments, as a result of what it described as its shift from individual AI use cases to “institutional capability”.

Read more about AI in finance

  • Evident research into artificial intelligence adoption in banking reveals US banks dominate when it comes to making AI work for the business.
  • AI-related roles could be the only ‘safe jobs’ in the banking sector as financial organisations ‘relentlessly’ press on with AI-led transformation.
  • The payment card services giant leads the way in applying artificial intelligence in its sector, according to research.

Mastercard came in at number two, while PayPal took third spot in the index of 12 payments companies, which documented nearly 100 use cases for AI in the payments sector.

But, according to Evident, payments firms have not detailed their return on investment from AI spend, unlike banks.

The index took into account four factors: talent, innovation, leadership and transparency. According to Evident, Visa demonstrates the clearest evidence that AI is institutionalised across its core transaction network.

“What sets Visa apart is the degree to which the company is demonstrating impact at scale over multiple years from applications of AI across its operations and network,” said Evident co-founder Alexandra Mousavizadeh at the time of the report. “It signals a shift from individual use cases to AI as an institutional capability.”

But unlike banks, Evident said no payments company has disclosed realised or projected return on investment across all AI investments. Also speaking at the time of the report, Evident’s other co-founder, Annabel Ayles, said this is “increasingly conspicuous”.

“While one in five banks now report on group-level AI returns, payments firms have yet to quantify the aggregate impact of their AI investments,” she said. “To keep justifying this expenditure, the market will sooner or later demand clearer evidence of value.”

Banks are gaining huge benefits from AI today, with Lloyds Banking Group’s Financial institutions sentiment survey for 2025 finding that 59% of surveyed firms reported AI-driven productivity gains in the past 12 months, compared with 32% in the 2024 survey.

title: The departmental deckchairs have been shuffled – but helping the government's tech challenge how?
raw_text:
It’s been a week since the axe fell on the Department for Science, Innovation and Technology (DSIT). What have we learned and, critically, are all things tech policy and delivery in a better place now than they were before the new prime minister’s cull?

It’s self-evident that when the department was brought into being it created a clear “route in” for tech businesses small and large and to all those looking for a simple point of access into government. This has now gone.

Last week in the House of Lords, we sought some rationale from the government for this move.

My colleague Tim Clement-Jones raised the issue, asking specifically what the implications would be for the future operation of organisations such as the AI Security Institute, the Government Digital Service (GDS) and UK Research and Innovation (UKRI).

The minister's response stressed that “science and AI are having an increasingly large impact on all areas of government policy and economic growth” and should not be seen as isolated from other areas.

This was given as the reasoning for what the minister described as “a bold restructuring, including the elevation of AI to the [newly established] Office for the Prime Minister and the Cabinet (OPMC).”

The government also published a Written Ministerial Statement setting out the changes, describing the redistribution of DSIT functions as designed to “align with our core economic and social agenda, embedded as vital engines of growth exactly where they can have the most direct impact.”

AI taskforce

There will be a new AI Taskforce within the OPMC, supported by the prime minister's adviser on AI, intended to implement “a strategic, whole-of-government approach [to AI] from the centre.” We now know that it will be Patrick Vallance – who recently departed from government as minister - who will chair this group. That is a very good thing and I hope he can gain traction and cut through in this landscape which has been rendered increasingly complex as a consequence of last week’s changes.

The Cabinet Office will take the lead on AI adoption across the Civil Service and will have responsibility for AI strategy, public sector AI adoption and the AI Security Institute.

Digital, with a capital D, returns to the renamed Department for Digital, Culture, Media and Sport (DCMS) which gains responsibility for “digital foundations, digital transformation, digital inclusion and skills, GDS, information resilience and online harms”. The government said that this will bring “coherence to the online safety agenda”.

The GDS move is particularly problematic. GDS built whatever authority it has over the last decade by sitting close enough to the centre to mandate standards across departments that would otherwise happily ignore it. The move to DCMS reduces GDS authority - GDS’s view - to that of a single department with the ability to, well, try and influence other departments of its view. If might is right, as is so often the case within Whitehall, the very best of British with that.

Just when you thought you had a grip on the departmental acronyms, another one emerges. The Department for Business and Trade is gone, becoming the Department for Business, Innovation, Science and Trade (DBIST), taking on responsibility for the science and innovation portfolio, as well as emerging sectors.

Keeping up so far? There’s more:

The Cabinet Office, having gained some new functions, will lose the Office for Equality and Opportunity, which moves to the Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government.

The Office for the Impact Economy and responsibility for policy on digital identity will move to DCMS.

The Public Sector Fraud Authority will move to the Department for Work and Pensions (DWP) with continued central sponsorship from HM Treasury. And the Investment Security Unit will move to DBIST.

Many questions

During our Lords debate, regret was expressed about the resignation of minister Vallance who will be much missed, though, as stated above, he has already re-appeared as the AI taskforce chair.

Many questions were raised about the changes, including responsibility for AI regulation, the "waste of time" and difficulties maintaining momentum on AI safety and sovereignty during the transition, the wrong signal being sent to the science community and the potential erosion of funding for basic science.

The severing of digital infrastructure from AI sovereign investment is also more than unfortunate. Prior to the change we had one department with effective oversight of these so clearly linked areas. This has been exchanged for a yet to be constructed coordination between different departments, with different ministers, with different incentives – is that really better?

It is positive that we are retaining Kanishka Narayan as AI minister and that he will attend Cabinet. But does he have a full picture of what is under his ministerial responsibility and who he reports to and in what order?

With all this change in Whitehall I do have cause to wonder whether a cross-sector, cross-economy AI regulation bill is more likely today than before the current PM’s arrival? Here’s hoping.

To conclude, I can’t improve upon the comments of Laura Gilbert, former director of the AI Incubator at Number 10, on hearing news of the changes:

"So now a new government has again come in, the very week that those affected by the last machinery of government [change] finally transitioned to new laptops, and what did they do? Did they arrive, ask questions, learn about what had not worked before and why, consult with people with government and technical expertise, understand the problems and carefully and thoughtfully design a solution? Or did they do the exact same thing the last two governments did to the exact same people, the thing that evidently they felt had failed to the point of needing fixing, and then pat themselves on the back?"

And, if they think it’s all over - it isn’t yet. As Commons Science, Innovation and Technology Select Committee chair Chi Onwurah said, she expects her committee to “look into the impact of closing DSIT, and how science, innovation and technology can best be coordinated across government in the absence of a dedicated department” in the autumn.

She welcomed the government’s ambition to embed science and tech across the economy but said splitting up DSIT risks “fragmenting” policies and “overloading departments that may lack capacity to give them the attention they need.”

That may well all be true, time et al will tell. One thing we can know for sure at this stage is that, as a consequence of the changes, when we all return in the autumn, the chair will be responsible for the BIST Select Committee in Parliament.

title: Bahrain cannot claim sovereign immunity for spyware attack against UK dissidents, top UK court rules
raw_text:
The Kingdom of Bahrain cannot claim sovereign immunity to legal action brought by two Bahraini dissidents who accuse it of infecting their computers with German-made spyware, the UK’s Supreme Court has ruled.

The dissidents, Saeed Shehabi and Moosa Mohammed, allege that the Kingdom of Bahrain infected their computers with FinFisher spyware while they were living in London in 2011.

The Supreme Court’s decision is expected to open the way for further legal action against countries that target people living in the UK with surveillance software, said Ida Aduwa, solicitor at law firm Leigh Day, which brought the case.

“This ruling sends a clear message to overseas states that use intrusive surveillance technology against peaceful political activists and others that they will face justice in the courts,” she said.

The Kingdom of Bahrain claimed that under the State Immunity Act 1978, sovereign states had immunity in cases where the perpetrators, or some of the acts, causing personal injury were not located in the UK.

But the Supreme Court, with a majority of three to two, found that modern technology enables surveillance to be carried out remotely, and that even if a foreign state conducted a surveillance operation from outside the UK, it would still involve an infringement of UK territorial sovereignty.

Shehabi, 71, a journalist and founder of Bahraini opposition party Al Wefaq, and Mohammed, a pro-democracy activist, allege that their laptops were infected in September 2011 with malicious surveillance software known as FinSpy, made by the Gamma group.

They claim the attacks allowed Bahraini authorities to collect information from their laptops, including messages, emails, calendar records, contact lists, browsing history, photos, databases, documents and videos. 

The software also enabled Bahrain to track the location of their laptops and covertly eavesdrop on conversations by using the laptop’s microphones and cameras.

The activists learned that their computers had been hacked in 2014 when WikiLeaks published documents about Bahrain’s use of FinSpy and a research and advocacy organisation, Bahrain Watch, identified them as victims of hacking.

Bahrain opposition to Shehabi and Mohammed

The Bahraini government has repeatedly denounced Shehabi – who has lived in the UK since 1973 and gained British citizenship in 2002 – over his political activism. In 2009, his home in the UK was set on fire shortly after two associates who had campaigned against the Bahraini government were beaten up outside London Euston railway station.

Mohammed, 45, a photographer, videographer and human rights activist, was repeatedly arrested, detained, tortured and mistreated by the police after taking part in protests in Bahrain. He fled to the UK in 2006 as a refugee, and has since been granted indefinite leave to remain in the UK.

The Bahraini government has publicly condemned him for helping to organise protests in the UK and publishing accounts of human rights abuses in the Kingdom.

In 2021, the Bahraini Ministry of Foreign Affairs included Shehabi and Mohammed on a list of Bahraini nationals who have had their Bahraini citizenship revoked.

Bahrain ‘can no longer hide’

Speaking after the verdict, Shehabi said the judgment means the Bahraini regime can no longer hide behind state immunity.

“This is not just a victory for us, but for everyone targeted by authoritarian states beyond their own borders,” he added. “The court’s message is clear: states that abuse people on British soil will be held accountable.”

Mohammed said the verdict changed the balance of power between Bahrain and dissidents.

“Since I was a teenager, the Bahraini regime has tortured, imprisoned and hunted me,” he said. “Even after I found safety in the UK, they pursued me across borders.”

Martyn Day, senior partner of law firm Leigh Day, which represented Shehabi and Mohammed, said the “notion that foreign governments can allegedly use sophisticated spyware to interfere with computers and mobile phones of people living in this country is an outrage”.

The law firm has previously represented people impacted by spyware from Rwanda, Saudi Arabia and Pakistan.

In the verdict today, Lord Lloyd-Jones, Lord Hamblen and Lady Simler found in favour of the two claimants. Lord Leggatt and Lord Burrows gave dissenting verdicts.

title: Nvidia pushes ahead with security alliance for AI openness
raw_text:
Nvidia has called on policymakers and business to support open artificial intelligence (AI) models to enable better cyber security.

It announced the industry-wide Open Secure AI just days after Microsoft’s open letter to US policymakers which described openness as “one of the most important paths to AI safety and security”.

In a blog post announcing the new initiative to drive open AI security, Nvidia said that companies and governments should invest in shared open infrastructure for AI defence – datasets, evaluation frameworks, attack simulators and red-teaming tools – similar to how past generations invested in open source software.

In the post, Nvidia said: “For cyber security, open models and open harnesses are essential because they democratise defensive capabilities, increase transparency for defenders, enable cyber defence while protecting data, and complement frontier closed models with customisable, localised controls. Open source enables massively distributed community-driven and self-controlled defence – with no single point of failure.”

The AI chipmaker has taken the decision to drive forward an industry alliance for open AI security, following the recent Hugging Face disclosure of a cyber attack that was driven from end-to-end by an autonomous AI agent system.

The advances in frontier AI models show that the tech sector is now in an arms race as advanced AI models continue to evolve.

Nvidia said the Hugging Face disclosure shows that cyber defence needs to be open, using frontier agentic systems: “When closed AI tools – unable to distinguish attackers from defenders – blocked essential forensic analysis, Hugging Face ran the open-weight GLM 5.2 model on its own infrastructure to analyse more than 17,000 actions and contain the intrusion.  

“That incident showed a practical truth: when defenders cannot inspect, adapt and run advanced AI on their own infrastructure, their ability to respond is constrained at exactly the moment speed matters most,” Nvidia warned. It said companies and countries need open frontier defensive tools and techniques to enable critical industries to build security systems across an ecosystem comprising multiple technology providers to  avoid single points of failure.

The inaugural members of the alliance are: Adobe, Cadence, Capital One, Cisco, Cloudera, Cloudflare, Cognition, CrowdStrike, Databricks, Dell Technologies, DoorDash, Elastic, HPE, Hugging Face, IBM, LangChain, the Linux Foundation, Microsoft, Naver, NetApp, Nous Research, OpenClaw, Palantir, Palo Alto Networks, Red Hat, Reflection AI, Salesforce, SAP, SK Telecom, ServiceNow, Siemens, Snowflake, SpacexAI, Synopsys, Thinking Machines Lab and TrendAI.

OpenUK has called on the UK to deliver a home-grown equivalent to the Linux Foundation to promote open source technologies. Its CEO Amanda Brock, said: “The alliance is an appropriate step reinforcing Friday’s open letter message to US policy makers and governments by Microsoft.

“It’s great to see a collective response to the open source security challenge – we’ve been seeing enterprises respond to these issues individually of late, but it’s primarily a US industry response. It’s another example of the future soft power that exists around AI.

“For the UK (like other middle nations) if we want a place at the future dinner table for AI, we need to carve out our own place now. That means sharing and collaborating, but from assets based on intellectual property and collaboration on the technologies that we evolve in country and in our own foundation.”

title: HSBC chooses Singapore for global AI centre of excellence
raw_text:
HSBC is launching an artificial intelligence (AI) centre of excellence in Singapore, with a plan to recruit 100 AI specialists.

The bank, like its competitors, has stepped up activity around AI. It appointed its first AI chief in March and recently signed a major AI-focused deal with Google Cloud.

In the second half of this year, it will begin developing AI capabilities in the centre, which can will be rolled out globally. Around 100 new roles will be created in the team of chief AI officer David Rice.

The bank announced Rice as its first AI chief as part of its wider plans to embed the technology across the company. He moved from his role as chief operating officer at the bank’s corporate and institutional bank.

Through the new centre, HSBC will focus on supporting staff in using AI to deliver customer services.

Georges Elhedery, group CEO at HSBC, said: “The new AI Centre of Excellence in Singapore will help drive our global AI vision – to empower our colleagues to use AI to create a personalised experience for each customer, deliver it safely, in real time and at scale, while keeping human judgement, decision-making and accountability at the core.”

The centre will kick-off with a focus on customer wealth journey conversations, agentic treasury functionality and AI-enabled digital payments.

In addition, the centre of excellence will build a pipeline of talent across natural language processing, data science, AI governance and human-centred design. As part of this, it will work with educational institutions and government bodies in Singapore.

Ramping up AI

Last month, HSBC announced plans to create more than 200 AI use cases across its business through a deal with Google Cloud, and it expects to make hundreds of millions of pounds in revenue and efficiency gains as a result.

The bank already had around 600 applications running on the Google Cloud service, but the new arrangement will see more than 200 AI use cases added in the next two years. It said it will prioritise the highest-value initiatives, where estimated value exceeds $100m.

As part of the agreement, HSBC will harness the skills of Google Cloud and Google DeepMind engineers, gaining access to Google’s agentic AI capabilities. Areas initially being focused on include highly personalising customer experience through AI, using the technology to manage financial crime risk and expanding the reach of an AI agent used by staff.

Banks are doubling down on AI, with HSBC the UK’s leader of the technology’s adoption. According to Evident’s Banking AI adoption index, which tracks financial services AI adoption, HSBC was the only UK bank in the top 10.

Banks can save huge amounts in operating costs through AI, but they must use it to improve customer experiences and offerings or face reduced profits. According to McKinsey’s latest report, while AI savings could be up to 20%, taking account of the cost of the technology, banking industry profits could fall 9% as customers move money based on AI agent recommendations.

“The impact of savings, while welcome, won’t last,” McKinsey said. “As with earlier innovations, competition will likely erode the gains for banks and most of the benefits will accrue to customers over time.”

According to Lloyds Banking Group’s Financial institutions sentiment survey for 2025 banks are gaining huge benefits from AI, stating that 59% of surveyed firms reported AI-driven productivity gains in the past 12 months, compared with 32% in the 2024 survey.

title: テルス・パワー、グリーンAIコンピューティング向け垂直型大規模モデル「テルス・エナジーAI」をローンチ
